description: RFC 3339 date / time / date-time PARSE conformance vectors for the MPP `expires` field, merged from four sources. EVERY scenario carries a `provenance` object naming where its input came from and what authority decided its verdict. Read `provenance.type` before trusting any row: `imported_verbatim` and `extracted_from_source` came from third-party test suites at a pinned commit; `hand_authored` and `derived_from_rfc_text` were written against the text of RFC 3339 and each carries the section that decides it.

scope.read_this_before_tests_parse: This corpus holds vectors for THREE different RFC 3339 productions, not one: `full-date` (a bare YYYY-MM-DD), `full-time` (a bare time with an offset), and `date-time` (full-date "T" full-time). Every scenario carries an `applies_to` field naming which of the three its verdict answers. Read `applies_to` before you read `tests.parse`. A verdict only means what it says inside its own production.

applies_to_values.full-date: The verdict answers RFC 3339 §5.6 `full-date` — a bare YYYY-MM-DD.
applies_to_values.full-time: The verdict answers RFC 3339 §5.6 `full-time` — a bare time with an offset.
applies_to_values.date-time: The verdict answers RFC 3339 §5.6 `date-time` = full-date "T" full-time. This is the production MPP `expires` holds.

scope.expires_holds_a_date_time: The MPP `expires` field holds a `date-time`. A `full-date` verdict and a `full-time` verdict are NOT `expires` verdicts. They are correct statements about a different production, imported verbatim from suites that test that production.
scope.an_expires_parser_is_correct_to_reject_f: An `expires` parser is CORRECT to reject every `full-date` input and every `full-time` input in this file. `2020-01-31` is not an `expires` value. `08:30:06Z` is not an `expires` value. If your parser rejects them, it is right and this corpus agrees with you. Do not file a bug against a parser for rejecting them, and do not "fix" a parser to accept them.

how_to_test_an_expires_implementation.rule: Filter to `applies_to == "date-time"` before running anything. That slice, and only that slice, is a set of `expires` verdicts. Running the unfiltered file against an `expires` parser will produce failures that are not defects.
how_to_test_an_expires_implementation.filter_python: expires_vectors = [s for s in corpus["scenarios"] if s["applies_to"] == "date-time"]

(Note the upstream case description, kept verbatim, reads "an invalid time string in date-time format" — that wording describes the input's shape, not the production being tested.)

Run unfiltered, it asserts that a correct SDK is broken. As an `expires` verdict it is inverted; as the `full-date` verdict it actually is, it is correct. Filtering to `applies_to == "date-time"` removes it. If you are looking at a mystified failure on `2020-11-28T23:55:45Z`, this paragraph is the answer.

source_notes.classification_rule: Every verdict here is decided by the text of RFC 3339 and by nothing else. Each shipped scenario carries an `rfc_ref` naming the section that decides it, and the verdict must follow from that section's text rather than from any parser's behaviour. Where the RFC and a widely-deployed parser disagree, the RFC governs and the disagreement is recorded under `rfc_vs_implementation_findings` below. A literal whose verdict cannot be pinned to a section is NOT shipped as a scenario; it is recorded in `disputed` instead. Every input literal in this corpus was written for this corpus from the RFC's own grammar; none is copied from another project's test data.
rfc_vs_implementation_findings: Lower-case 't' and 'z' separators. The §5.6 NOTE states that the "T" and "Z" characters in this syntax may alternatively be lower case "t" or "z", so RFC 3339 ACCEPTS them; the same section adds that applications which GENERATE this format SHOULD use upper case, which is a generation constraint and not a parse constraint. Parsers built against a fixed upper-case layout string reject them. The three lowercase_* vectors here are ACCEPT on the RFC's authority, and this NOTE is the only thing that makes them ACCEPT rather than REJECT.

Leap second (time-second = 60). §5.7 permits time-second = 60 at the end of months in which a leap second occurs, and the §5.8 worked examples carry 1990-12-31T23:59:60Z and its -08:00 restatement verbatim, so RFC 3339 ACCEPTS. Parsers backed by a calendar type with no representable 61st second reject it as out of range. The four leap-second vectors here are ACCEPT on the RFC's authority.

Fractional digits beyond nine. §5.6 time-secfrac = "." 1*DIGIT sets a lower bound of one digit and no upper bound, so any digit count is ACCEPT as grammar. Implementations backed by a fixed nanosecond field truncate at nine, and implementations that accumulate the fraction into a signed 64-bit integer before scaling overflow at nineteen digits. Neither behaviour is encoded in these verdicts; secfrac_10_digits and secfrac_19_digits_exceeds_int64 exercise both boundaries.

hand_authoring_rule.boundary_rule: A boundary vector without its counterpart tests nothing. Each boundary below is authored with both sides present -- either both sides are authored here, or the counterpart already ships in a named file and that file is named in the scenario description.
hand_authoring_rule.deliberately_not_authored: Classes already covered elsewhere, and questions the RFC does not decide, are listed in the S5 result document rather than given a verdict here. scenarios.name: offset_max_syntactic_plus_23_59
scenarios.description: Maximum SYNTACTIC offset. §5.6 gives time-numoffset = ("+" / "-") time-hour ":" time-minute, with time-hour = 2DIGIT ; 00-23 and time-minute = 2DIGIT ; 00-59, so +23:59 is the largest offset the grammar generates. This is well outside the range of any real timezone. The REJECT counterpart one minute above this boundary already ships as `offset_hour_out_of_range` (2026-01-29T12:00:00+24:00) in expires-rfc3339.json. NOTE for consumers: the offsets named as extremes in the upstream issue, +14:00 and -12:00, are the TIMEZONE extremes and already ship as `offset_plus_fourteen` and `offset_minus_twelve`; they are not the grammar's extremes. An implementation that range-checks offsets against tz data rather than against §5.6 will reject this conforming input. The base date is mid-range so that the offset-adjusted instant cannot overflow date-fullyear, which is a separate and deliberately undecided question held in the `disputed` block of expires-rfc3339.json.

scenarios.name: offset_min_syntactic_minus_23_59
scenarios.description: Minimum SYNTACTIC offset, the negative arm of the same §5.6 boundary. time-numoffset admits ("+" / "-") equally, so -23:59 is as conforming as +23:59. The REJECT counterpart on this arm already ships in import-json-schema-test-suite.json as `jsts_date_time_011` (1990-12-31T15:59:59-24:00, upstream valid:false), where the offset hour 24 exceeds time-hour's 00-23 range. Together with offset_max_syntactic_plus_23_59 this closes the last-legal / first-illegal pair on both signs.

scenarios.name: leap_second_offset_rolls_local_date_forward
scenarios.description: A leap second in date-time form where the zone offset pushes the LOCAL date across midnight. §5.7: "Further, in time zones other than 'Z', the leap second point is shifted by the zone offset (so it happens at the same instant around the globe)." 1999-01-01T00:59:60+01:00 resolves to 1998-12-31T23:59:60Z, which is the final row of the Appendix D leap second table and which already ships as an ACCEPT in three files. The only variable this vector changes is that the local date reads 1999-01-01 while the UTC date is 1998-12-31, so the leap second no longer sits at a visible month end. §5.7's month-end condition is a condition on the UTC instant, which the shifting sentence makes explicit. This is the case an implementation gets wrong when it validates the :60 against the LOCAL date rather than the offset-adjusted one. No vector in expires-rfc3339.json, import-json-schema-test-suite.json or import-go-stdlib.json rolls the date: every other date-time :60 vector keeps the local and UTC dates equal, because §5.8's worked example 1990-12-31T15:59:60-08:00 uses a negative offset that cannot roll forward, and a bare full-time has no date to roll.

provenance.rfc_ref: RFC 3339 §5.7 (leap second point is shifted by the zone offset) + Appendix D (1998-12-31 leap second table row)

scenarios.name: leap_second_offset_rolls_local_date_forward_wrong_offset
scenarios.description: The REJECT counterpart of leap_second_offset_rolls_local_date_forward, and the reason that vector proves anything. Character for character this differs only in the offset hour: 1999-01-01T00:59:60+02:00 resolves to 1998-12-31T22:59:60Z, which is not the leap second point. §5.7: "At all other times the maximum value of time-second is '59'." An implementation that accepts the ACCEPT vector by ignoring the offset entirely, rather than by applying it, will also accept this one -- so the pair distinguishes offset-aware handling from a blanket :60 permission. Both sides of the boundary are authored here.

provenance.rfc_ref: RFC 3339 §5.7 ("At all other times the maximum value of time-second is '59'"; leap second point is shifted by the zone offset)

disputed.reason: RFC 3339 §5.6 ABNF is date-time = full-date "T" full-time, which mandates a literal "T". But the second NOTE in the same section reads: "ISO 8601 defines date and time separated by 'T'. Applications using this syntax may choose, for the sake of readability, to specify a full-date and full-time separated by (say) a space character." The NOTE neither amends the date-time production (as the lower-case NOTE explicitly does) nor states that the space form is a valid date-time. The verdict therefore cannot be pinned to a single section.

Second = 60 on a date that is not a June or December month end. §5.7 permits time-second = 60 "at the end of months in which a leap second occurs -- to date: June (XXXX-06-30T23:59:60Z) or December (XXXX-12-31T23:59:60Z)" and adds "At all other times the maximum value of time-second is 59". Read as a grammar restriction that is REJECT; but the same section says leap seconds "cannot be predicted far into the future" and are announced by IERS bulletin, and §5.7 records that first preference is June/December and SECOND preference March/September (Appendix D). Whether a parser is expected to enforce the month restriction, or only the 00-60 range, is not settled by the text.

Second = 60 at a June month end in a year for which no leap second was announced. Positionally this is exactly the shape §5.7 names as permitted (XXXX-06-30T23:59:60Z), so a grammar-only reading ACCEPTS. But §5.7 conditions the permission on "months in which a leap second occurs", and no leap second occurred at 2026-06-30. A parser cannot hold the IERS bulletin history, so the section cannot decide this literal. Contrast the two SHIPPED leap-second vectors, which use 1972-06-30 and 1998-12-31 -- both rows of the Appendix D table, where the leap second demonstrably did occur.

Surrounding whitespace. RFC 3339 §5.6 defines the date-time production and nothing else; it does not say whether a protocol field carrying a date-time may be padded. Whether the padding is stripped before the value reaches the parser is a question about the carrying protocol's field-value semantics, not about RFC 3339. No RFC 3339 section decides it.

Lexically valid date-times whose offset-adjusted UTC instant falls outside the four-digit year range (year 10000 and year -0001 respectively). §5.6 date-fullyear = 4DIGIT constrains the LEXICAL year only. §5.7 restricts date-mday and time-second and says nothing about whether the offset-adjusted instant must also remain representable. Grammatically ACCEPT, semantically an overflow. No section decides which reading governs.
